entry.title: Automate Datasphere Objects' transport with datasphere-cli
entry.content:
SAP Datasphere #DevOps #Transport #Automation #Git

Overview:
SAP Datasphere provides built-in transport capabilities for promoting artifacts between tenants along with cTMS which is another tool that can be leverage for objects promotions across a multi-tier landscape. However, for teams already working with Git-based workflows where peer review, branching strategies, version control and deployment pipelines are standard practice, there is a natural desire to bring that same discipline to Datasphere artifact lifecycle management.

This blog describes how SAP Datasphere CLI (@sap/datasphere-cli) can be used to build a lightweight, Git-native transport pipeline that fits into existing developer workflows and automates this process end-to-end.

Followed Approach:
The pipeline is built around a simple principle: Git as the intermediary or staging layer. Artifacts are exported from a source Datasphere tenant, versioned in GitLab, and imported into a target tenant, all via scripted datasphere-cli calls. No manual file handling, no browser exports.

The workflow runs in two directions:

  1. DSP → Git (Pull): A dedicated script connects to the source tenant, discovers all artifacts by specified types, and compares the full content hash of each artifact against the locally stored version. Only genuinely changed artifact or new artifacts are written to an export folder. Once the pull completes, the developer reviews the changes in VS Code Source Control, selects which files to stage, and pushes to GitLab giving full control and flexibility over what gets pulled from Datasphere and versioned.
  2. Git → DSP (Push): A second script scans Git history for changed/new files and presents an interactive numbered list, allowing the user to select exactly which artifacts to transport. It then imports each artifact into the target tenant using datasphere-cli create command, falling back to update on conflict, and verifies each import with a post-import read. A full audit log captures every outcome.

How does datasphere-cli make it possible?
Beyond artifact transport, datasphere-cli exposes a broad set of capabilities that can be leveraged to automate surrounding workflows:

  • Artifact lifecycle: discover, read, create, update across all major object types including local tables, views, replication flows and analytic models
  • Package management: list, create, update, read and export package definitions for dependency-aware transport
  • CI/CD integration: the pipeline can be fully automated as every transport operation runs without manual intervention, making it straightforward to integrate into existing CI/CD workflows.

Workflow diagram:

Pre-requisites: 

  • SAP Datasphere tenant(s)
  • OAuth client credentials configured in SAP Datasphere, with Interactive Usage
  • SAP Datasphere CLI installed 
  • Git repository (GitLab or GitHub)
  • Python 3.9 or above

Authentication: 

  1. SAP Datasphere Access is maintained using an OAuth client (client ID and secret) created in Datasphere tenant. These credentials can be stored in the config file or as environment variables which is recommended to avoid storing secrets in plain text. datasphere-cli establishes a session on first run and caches it locally, so subsequent runs reuse the existing session without re-authenticating.
  2. GitLab Access is authenticated using a Personal Access Token generated in GitLab. The token is stored in Windows Credential Manager and picked up automatically by Git on every push and pull, with no configuration needed in the scripts.

Dependency Ordering
Transporting multiple artifacts in the right order is crucial as a view cannot be imported before the table it references. By leveraging datasphere-cli objects packages list, create, read and export commands, package manifests can be pulled alongside artifacts. These manifests capture which objects belong to each package and their dependencies, enabling the pipeline to resolve the correct import sequence automatically using a topological sort. Teams that organise their artifacts into Datasphere packages benefit from fully automatic dependency ordering with no manual sequencing required.

Change Detection
Two approaches are supported for detecting whether an artifact has changed since the last pull:

  1. Hash comparison: computes a SHA-256 hash of the full artifact content and compares it against the locally stored version. Only genuine content changes trigger a write. This is the recommended default.
  2. Timestamp comparison: compares Datasphere's internal deployment timestamp against the local file. Less precise as redeploying an object in Datasphere without structural changes still updates its timestamp, triggering an unnecessary write.

Audting:
Every action (pull, push) is written to a structured log file with a timestamp, status, and detail, making it straightforward to trace what happened and when across any transport run.

Important Considerations:

  • Authentication Expiry: OAuth client credentials configured for each tenant have a maximum validity period of 180 days. Once expired, all pipeline operations (pull, push) will fail to authenticate. It is recommended to track the expiry date of each client credential and renew them in advance to avoid unexpected transport failures.
  • Merge requests/pre-import conflict detection: Before importing, the pipeline checks whether the artifact already exists in the target space. Three outcomes are possible: the artifact is new and gets created, it exists with identical content and is skipped, or it exists with different content and the operator is prompted to resolve the conflict before proceeding.
  • Credentials handling (e.g connections, access tokens): Connection definitions can be transported as part of the pipeline, credentials are never stored in the exported artifact but can be retrieved securely at import time from a secrets manager (e.g. AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, etc) keeping the transport fully automated without exposing sensitive credentials in Git.
  • Transport across spaces: The same pipeline logic applies to transporting artifacts across spaces within the same tenant. Rather than pointing the source and target configurations to different tenants, both can be configured with the same host but different space IDs. Pull, conflict detection, and push all behave identically. Git remains a useful intermediary in this scenario, providing a version-controlled audit trail of what moved between spaces and when.
  • Scalability and performance: Initial tests covered local tables, views, and flows transported individually and as part of a package with consistent results. For larger spaces, performance scales linearly as artifacts are processed one at a time, and future iterations could address this through parallelisation and batched API calls. For high-volume migrations, a performance comparison against cTMS would be a worthwhile exercise and the right choice ultimately depends on whether the team favours a Git-native workflow or centrally managed package releases.

Conclusion:
This approach is not a replacement for Datasphere's native transport capabilities or cTMS. It is a solution for teams running Datasphere through automation or DevOps pipelines. Version control, branching, code review, and automated deployment are now part of how Datasphere artifacts can be managed, all made possible through datasphere-cli.

entry.title: Your data has layers, most data teams see only one
entry.content:
Your data has layers, most data teams see only one

 

The Terminology Problem

"Master data," "semantics," and "context" appear in almost every data architecture and governance conversation. They show up in vendor pitches, platform documentation, and cross-functional design sessions, often used interchangeably and rarely defined with any precision. For a data steward, analyst, or engineer trying to build something that actually works, that imprecision has real consequences. SAP has specific, deliberate definitions for each of these terms, and those definitions connect directly to how its data solutions are built and how they fit together. Getting precise about the language is not a mere naming exercise. It is the difference between an architecture that holds and one that quietly fails at the seams.

The three layers of data: what they are and what each one addresses

Master Data: The Foundation

SAP defines master data as the core business entities that give your processes their meaning and continuity: customers, suppliers, products, materials, employees, locations, etc. These are the nouns of your business. They do not change with every transaction, but everything important depends on them being accurate, consistent, and trusted across every system that touches them.

In the SAP portfolio, two solutions address master data from different angles. SAP Master Data Governance (MDG) governs master data at the SAP core, enforcing policies, managing change request workflows, and maintaining data stewardship inside core business processes. SAP Reltio approaches it from the enterprise perspective. It takes records from SAP, Salesforce, Oracle, legacy ERPs, and any other system in your landscape, identifies which records represent the same real-world entity, and produces a unified, trusted consolidated profile available to every downstream system, analytical tool, and AI agent.

In an Order to Cash process, when a sales order comes in for Acme Corp, the master data is the foundation: the customer record carrying the name, billing address, payment terms, preferred delivery method, and credit limit. SAP MDG ensures that record was created and maintained correctly inside SAP. SAP Reltio ensures that the Acme Corp record sitting in your CRM and used in the Order to Cash business process is recognized as the same, trusted entity used in downstream analytics and AI, not a duplicate or a shadow record living a separate life in a parallel system.

Semantics: The Meaning Layer

Master data tells you what your entities are. Semantics tells you what they mean.

SAP defines semantics as the business meaning assigned to data: the definitions, relationships, and rules that transform a technical data structure into something a business process can understand and act on. A field named "KUNNR" in SAP S/4HANA means nothing to a data scientist pulling it into a model. A semantically enriched version of that same field tells a different story. It is labeled "Customer Number," typed as an identifier, linked to the Customer entity, and given valid value ranges. That version is immediately useful.

This is the space that SAP Datasphere, the data integration and management layer within SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC), is designed for. The semantic layer in SAP Datasphere lets data teams define what data means in business terms, independent of the underlying technical structure. You model entities, attributes, and relationships at the business level, and that semantic model becomes the common language between your source systems and every analytical or operational consumer downstream.

Back in the Order to Cash scenario: Acme Corp's master record has a credit limit field. Semantics define what that field means in practice. It represents the maximum outstanding balance in USD before new orders are blocked, it is linked to the credit exposure calculation, and it triggers a specific pricing tier. Without that semantic layer, a data analyst pulling credit data from three different systems has no reliable way of knowing whether she is comparing the same thing.

Context: The Situational Layer

Semantics tells you what your data means in general. Context tells you what it means right now, in this process, for this decision.

SAP defines context as the situational information that gives data its relevance: the process it is embedded in, the time it was captured, the relationships it holds to other data points at a specific moment. Context is what transforms a well-defined, semantically accurate data asset into something you can act on.

SAP Business Data Cloud addresses context at an architectural level. By integrating master data, transactional data, analytical data, and operational metadata inside a curated data product, SAP BDC allows every piece of data to be understood in relation to the business processes around it. Not as an isolated record, but as part of a live operational picture.

In the Order to Cash scenario, context is what tells you that Acme Corp currently has $85,000 of their $100,000 credit limit utilized, that two invoices are overdue, that their contract was renewed last week, and that the sales rep submitted a priority flag on the account this morning. The master data has not changed. The semantic definitions have not changed. But the context is different from last month, and it should change how this order is handled.

This is the transactional layer of context: the live operational state that gives data its situational relevance. The broader business context layer goes further, encoding process intelligence, institutional memory, unstructured document knowledge, and AI governance constraints. Together, those elements form a complete picture of how an enterprise operates and what its AI agents are permitted to do. That conversation deserves its own post (and it is available here, Why Your AI Strategy Needs a Robust Business Context).

How the Three Layers Connect

These three terms describe three distinct layers of a complete data architecture, and each one depends on the one beneath it.

Master data is the what: the trusted entities your business runs on. Semantics is the meaning: the definitions and relationships that make those entities interpretable across systems and teams. Context is the relevance: the situational lens that makes data actionable in a specific moment and process.

When one layer is missing or broken, the layers above it fail. Imprecise master data produces semantically rich models of unreliable entities. Clear semantics over untrustworthy master data gives you well-labeled friction. And accurate master data with solid semantics but no contextual layer leaves your AI agents and analytics tools making decisions without the situational intelligence they need to get it right.

SAP MDG and SAP Reltio address the master data layer, governance at the SAP core and unification across the enterprise. SAP Datasphere addresses the semantics layer, translating technical structures into business-meaningful models. SAP Business Data Cloud addresses context, connecting the data layers into a unified architecture where everything is understood in relation to everything else.

For the data professional building or operating within this stack, the practical takeaway is straightforward: the quality of your outputs, whether that is an analytics dashboard, an AI-generated recommendation, or an automated process decision, depends on how well all three layers are working. Not just one of them.

Where This Gets Real

I have watched teams spend months on semantic modeling while their master data was still fragmented across five systems. The layers look independent on a diagram, but they are not in practice. If you are working through this in your own environment, I would genuinely like to hear where the friction is. Drop a comment below or follow along. This is a conversation worth having.

entry.title: Which Browser Is Best for SAP Analytics?
entry.content:
It seems like yesterday, but it's been seven years since I last wrote about browser support for SAP Analytics. In 2019, we were watching the slow death of Microsoft Internet Explorer and the massive adoption of Google Chrome.

Cover image: Dashboard screenshot courtesy of InfoSol. View additional dashboard examples at https://www.infosol.com/dashboard-gallery/

 

Today, there is a nearly endless supply of browsers, but only three major browser rendering engines - all of which are open source: Blink (used by Chromium-based browsers), WebKit (used primarily by Apple's Safari), and Gecko (used primarily by Mozilla Firefox).

EngineMaintainerMajor Browsers
BlinkGoogleGoogle Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Brave, Vivaldi, Arc, DuckDuckGo Browser (Windows), Ace Browser, and most other Chromium-based browsers.
WebKitAppleSafari, plus all browsers on iOS and iPadOS (including iOS versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Opera, which are required by Apple to use WebKit).
GeckoMozillaFirefox, Tor Browser, Mullvad Browser, LibreWolf, Waterfox, and other Firefox-derived browsers.

Which Browsers are Supported for SAP Analytics Cloud?

The supported browsers for SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC) can be found on SAP Help Portal. SAC supports both Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, which share the same Chromium foundation.

Mobile users should use the SAP Analytics Cloud mobile app, as mobile browsers are not supported.

  • Download Google Chrome
  • Download Microsoft Edge
  • Download SAP Analytics Cloud for iOS
  • Download SAP Analytics Cloud for Android

Which Browsers are Supported for SAP BusinessObjects?

The supported browsers for SAP BusinessObjects can be found in its Platform Availability Matrix (PAM). In addition to Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, there is support for Apple Safari and Mozilla Firefox.

Mobile users can access SAP BusinessObjects through mobile browsers, as the SAP BusinessObjects Mobile application was removed from SAP BusinessObjects BI 2025 (see SAP KB 3557283).

Note that WIDX support in BI 2025 is limited to Windows desktop browsers with Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge.

  • Download Google Chrome
  • Download Microsoft Edge
  • Download Apple Safari
  • Download Mozilla Firefox

Help SAP Support Help You

Ever encounter an issue worth reporting to SAP Support? Be sure to include the browser name and version in your incident. If possible, try the other supported browsers. Some issues affect all browsers. Others are unique to a specific browser. I've even encountered a situation where an issue in Microsoft Edge did not occur in Google Chrome despite their shared Chromium foundation.

 
Choosing the Right Browser

If you'd asked me in 2019 which browser would win, I would have answered Google Chrome. In 2026, the answer is more nuanced. Chrome remains dominant, but Edge has become a strong alternative. For SAP BusinessObjects, Firefox continues to provide an independent engine, and Safari remains essential for Apple users.

My personal preference is Microsoft Edge, as my bookmarks synchronize with my Microsoft 365 account. Google Chrome offers similar functionality, but I find Edge integrates more naturally into a Microsoft-centric work environment.

Whatever your preference, browser testing remains an important part of supporting SAP Analytics solutions. Never assume that behavior in one browser guarantees identical behavior in another.

entry.title: From AI-Ready Data to Agent-Ready Data
entry.content:
Agent Ready Data Series :

01  From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data

02  Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent

03  Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas

For years, many data architecture conversations started with the same question: How do we bring data together so the business can report on it?

With AI agents, I think we need to add another question:

What does an agent need to understand before we allow it to recommend — or take — an action?

A dashboard may tell us that overdue receivables have increased. An agent could go much further. It might be asked to identify the customers behind the increase, check disputed invoices, recommend the next step, and even create a follow-up task.

That is a very different demand on the data foundation. Every one of those steps requires more than a clean table.

What changes for the data foundation?

An agent needs to understand the agreed meaning of a measure such as DSO. It needs to know the relationships between customers, invoices, and disputes. It needs to understand where each figure came from, how fresh it is, and which permissions apply to both the user and the agent.

Just as importantly, there needs to be a clear boundary between explaining a situation and changing it.

An AI response can sound completely convincing even when one of these foundations is missing.

Gartner describes the move toward agent-ready data in terms of whether data is suitable for agentic use and whether the agent is using it in a valid way. McKinsey also emphasizes semantics, reusable data products, relationships, governance, and observability.

I find both perspectives useful because they move the discussion away from a broad statement such as “our data is clean” and toward something much more specific:

Is this data ready for this agent, this user, this decision, and this action?

How I would approach this in an SAP landscape

SAP Business Data Cloud and its data products can provide a governed starting point.

SAP Datasphere can help model business meaning and make data easier to discover and consume.

SAP Knowledge Graph also appears in SAP’s longer-term architecture vision as a semantic grounding layer for agents. I would treat that as architectural direction rather than assuming that every capability is already available in every customer landscape today.

If I were starting a customer workshop, I would begin with five questions:

  1. What decision should the agent support?
  2. Which facts would an experienced employee check before making that decision?
  3. Who owns the definitions and quality checks behind those facts?
  4. What is the agent allowed to see and do?
  5. How will we trace its answer back to the supporting evidence?

The answers to those questions tell us what data products, semantics, documents, and controls are actually required.

For a first release, I would often start with an agent that explains a situation and cites the supporting records.

If users can validate the answer consistently, we can then assess whether a controlled action makes sense.

This is where I see the role of the data architect evolving. Our job is no longer only to deliver the right number. We also need to establish its meaning, reliability, context, and permitted use inside a business process.

A practical way to make this real is to start small: one question, one user role, and one proposed action.

That makes the architecture testable.

If the answer changes when the role or proposed action changes, the underlying data product may still be valuable, but the agent design probably needs a more precise boundary.

This also gives the architect an important role in adoption conversations.

We can bring finance, process, security, and data teams around one concrete scenario and make their assumptions visible. If they disagree, that disagreement is useful evidence. It tells us where the design is still unclear.

It is much cheaper to resolve those questions in a workshop than after an automated action has already been taken.

entry.title: Need to Know: SAP Business Data Cloud
entry.content:
Need to Know: SAP Business Data Cloud

A plain English guide for SAP customers — what it is, what it does, and why it matters

 

What Is SAP Business Data Cloud — And Why Should SAP Customers Care?

SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) is a fully managed, cloud-based solution that brings all of your SAP data — and data from other systems — together in one governed, intelligent platform. Introduced in February 2025, it acts as the single source of truth for your business data, built specifically for organisations already running SAP.

For years, many SAP customers have struggled with data spread across multiple systems — finance in one place, HR in another, supply chain somewhere else. Making sense of it all often meant expensive extract-and-replicate processes that stripped away the original business meaning of the data.

BDC solves this by keeping data connected to its business context — the "what does this number actually mean?" layer that gets lost when data is moved around. It does this without forcing you to rip out your existing SAP landscape. Whether you are running S/4HANA, SAP BW, SAP Datasphere, or SAP Analytics Cloud, BDC is designed to extend and modernise what you already have, not replace it.

The result is a trusted data foundation that supports better analytics, smarter decisions, and — increasingly — AI-powered automation across your business.

 

SAP Managed Data Products — And What Do They Mean for You?

One of the most practical features of SAP Business Data Cloud is something called managed data products. The name sounds technical, but the idea is straightforward.

A managed data product is a pre-built, ready-to-use package of business data — curated by SAP — that comes complete with its business meaning, governance rules, and the context needed to use it straight away. Rather than pulling raw data out of your SAP systems and spending weeks figuring out what it means, data products do that work for you upfront.

 

For existing SAP customers, this is significant. Here is why:

  • No more rebuilding context: Data products carry the business definitions and semantics directly from your SAP source systems — so a "revenue" figure in BDC means the same thing as it does in S/4HANA.
  • Means all SAP Cloud Solutions: Managed data products means that SAP will extract from all SAP Cloud solutions including S/4HANA RISE, S/4 Public Cloud, SuccessFactors, Ariba, Concur and SAP Customer Experience CX cloud solutions.
  • Faster time to insight: Because data products are pre-curated and governed, your analytics and reporting teams can start using them immediately, without lengthy data preparation cycles.
  • Reusable across your business: The same data product can support dashboards, planning, and AI use cases — built once, used many times.
  • Data stored as industry standard data products: SAP store the data in the Hana Data Lake in a standard data lakehouse format, meaning cheaper storage and compatibility with other data lakes via Business Data Cloud Connect – see below for more information.
  • Your own custom products too: Alongside SAP-delivered data products, customers can create their own — for example, turning existing SAP BW objects into governed, reusable assets within BDC.  See the next section to learn more.

 

What Are Customer-Managed Data Products — And Why Do They Matter?

In the previous section we covered SAP-managed data products — the pre-built, SAP-curated datasets that come ready to use out of the box. But SAP Business Data Cloud also gives you the ability to build your own. These are called customer-managed data products, and they are just as important.

A customer-managed data product is a governed, reusable dataset that your organisation builds and owns — tailored to your specific business processes and data. Think of it as taking the same principles behind SAP-managed data products (context, governance, reusability) and applying them to data that is unique to your business.

For existing SAP customers, this opens up some practical possibilities:

  • Modernise your SAP BW investment: Existing SAP Business Warehouse objects can be converted into governed, cloud-based customer-managed data products — preserving years of accumulated business logic without starting from scratch.
  • Publish custom S/4HANA data: Operational data from SAP S/4HANA — such as orders, financials, or supply chain — can be packaged as a governed data product and shared across your organisation.  This is ideal for S/4HANA on-premise solutions, giving you a quick and easy way to use this data as data products.
  • Combine SAP and non-SAP data: You can build data products that blend SAP data with data from other systems, creating a single trusted asset for reporting or AI.
  • Reduce repetitive work: Once built, a customer-managed data product can be reused across multiple use cases — dashboards, planning models, AI — without rebuilding the same logic each time.

In short, customer-managed data products let you apply the same rigour and structure of SAP's own data products to the parts of your data landscape that are uniquely yours.

 

What if I have SAP Business Warehouse?  SAP Business Warehouse Modernisation — A Practical Path Forward

For many organisations, SAP Business Warehouse (BW) has been the backbone of their reporting and analytics for years — sometimes decades. It holds valuable business logic, carefully built data models, and years of accumulated knowledge. The challenge is that traditional on-premises BW is aging, and mainstream support for classic SAP BW 7.5 is scheduled to end in 2027.

SAP Business Data Cloud is SAP's stated path forward for these customers. Importantly, it is not about scrapping what you have built. Instead, BDC lets you modernise gradually — on your terms.

Here is what that looks like in practice:

  • Host BW in the cloud: Existing SAP BW instances can be hosted as a Private Cloud Edition within BDC, keeping your current environment running while you plan the next steps.
  • Convert BW objects into data products: Rather than rebuilding from scratch, you can turn existing BW objects into governed, reusable customer-managed data products — preserving the business logic already embedded in them.
  • Move at your own pace: BDC supports a phased approach. You can migrate high-value BW content first, retire what is no longer needed, and transition the rest incrementally over time.
  • Unlock new capabilities: Once your BW data sits within BDC, you gain access to modern features such as AI-ready analytics, bidirectional data sharing, and integration with platforms like SAP Datasphere and SAP Analytics Cloud.

For SAP BW customers, the message is clear: BDC is not a forced migration — it is a structured, lower-risk way to modernise while protecting the investment you have already made.

 

BDC Connect — Bringing Your SAP Data to the Platforms You Already Use

One of the most practical questions any SAP customer asks is: "We already use Databricks / Snowflake / Microsoft Fabric — do we have to give that up?" SAP Business Data Cloud Connect is the answer.

BDC Connect is SAP's zero-copy, bidirectional data sharing layer. It allows governed SAP data products — complete with their business context and semantics — to be shared directly into the platforms your teams already work in, without physically copying or replicating data. This eliminates the costly, fragile ETL pipelines that have traditionally been needed to move SAP data into external tools.

SAP has built BDC Connect integrations with the industry's leading data and cloud platforms:

  • Databricks: The first live BDC Connect partner. SAP data products can be shared bidirectionally into Databricks environments using the open Delta Sharing protocol — preserving governance and business meaning, with no replication required.
  • Snowflake: BDC Connect for Snowflake became generally available in May 2026. Existing Snowflake customers can access SAP data products directly in their Snowflake environment, and share data back into BDC — all with zero-copy, semantics-preserving connectivity.
  • Google Cloud (BigQuery): SAP and Google Cloud have announced BDC Connect for BigQuery, enabling bidirectional, zero-copy access to SAP data products across BDC and BigQuery — reducing silos and preserving business context for analytics and AI workloads.
  • Microsoft Fabric: SAP has announced BDC Connect for Microsoft Fabric, enabling SAP business data to flow into Microsoft's unified analytics platform — including OneLake, Copilot Studio, and Azure AI Foundry — without creating data copies.
  • Amazon Web Services (AWS): SAP and AWS allow you to connect BDC data with AWS data again with zero copy and zero movement.

 

 
 

 

 

 

What this means for data science and AI?

BDC Connect is not just a data pipeline — it is a foundation for trusted AI. When your data scientists and AI teams work in Databricks, Snowflake, or BigQuery, they are no longer working with stale extracts stripped of business meaning. They work with live, governed, semantically rich SAP data products.

This matters because AI models are only as good as the data they are built on. With BDC Connect, machine learning models, predictive analytics, and AI agents can consume SAP data — finance, supply chain, HR, and more — with full business context intact, directly within the tools your teams already use.

 

SAP Analytics Cloud and SAP Datasphere — Where Do They Fit?

Two products sit at the heart of SAP Business Data Cloud that are worth understanding in their own right: SAP Datasphere and SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC). Whether you already use them or not, they are directly relevant to how BDC delivers value.

What each one does:

  • SAP Datasphere: The data integration and semantic modelling layer within BDC. It connects SAP and non-SAP data sources, applies business meaning to that data, and makes it available as governed, trusted data products across your organisation.
  • SAP Analytics Cloud: Where that trusted data is consumed — delivering dashboards, reporting, planning, and AI-powered analytics in a single solution, all connected directly to the governed data foundation provided by Datasphere.  Also, SAP Analytics Cloud is not just a great analytics tool, it is the planning budgeting and forecasting solution that SAP recommends.  Coupled with Business Data Cloud you can now host the planning data inside the Datasphere models (something called Seamless Planning) meaning less movement and great integration of data.

Together, they form the analytics backbone of SAP Business Data Cloud.

If you already use SAP Analytics Cloud or SAP Datasphere:

Your existing investment is protected. SAP is clear that current SAC and Datasphere customers can continue using their services without interruption. Over time, BDC provides a natural upgrade path — extending what you already have with a more fully managed, governed foundation, richer data products, and deeper AI capabilities — without requiring a disruptive restart.

If you do not yet have SAP Analytics Cloud or SAP Datasphere:

SAP Business Data Cloud is the most complete way to adopt both. Rather than purchasing and implementing them individually, BDC brings SAP Datasphere, SAP Analytics Cloud, SAP BW, and SAP Databricks together in a single, fully managed SaaS solution — giving you SAP's full modern analytics and data platform from day one, already integrated and ready to use.

 

Finally, how SAP Business Data Cloud fits into the SAP Business AI Platform

At SAP Sapphire 2026, SAP introduced the SAP Autonomous Suite or Enterprise and the Business AI Platform — a unified foundation for building, connecting, and governing AI across the enterprise. SAP Business Data Cloud sits at the very heart of it.

 

The platform is built around three pillars:

  • Build: The development layer where organisations and partners create, extend, and deploy AI agents, applications, and workflows — built on the capabilities of the former SAP Business Technology Platform.
  • Contextualise and Reason: The intelligence layer that grounds AI in real business data, process logic, relationships, and policies — so AI agents understand your business, not just your prompts.
  • Govern: The control layer that manages the lifecycle, compliance, access, and auditability of AI assets across the enterprise.

See the blog Need to Know - The SAP Business AI Platform Overview Guide for an overview of this. 

The Contextualise and Reason Pillar including the SAP Knowledge Graph

Of the three pillars, Contextualise and Reason is where SAP Business Data Cloud plays its most critical role and where the SAP Knowledge Graph becomes especially important for existing SAP customers.

The SAP Knowledge Graph is a machine-readable map of your business. It encodes how SAP processes, entities, and relationships connect — for example, how a purchase requisition flows through approval to a purchase order, goods receipt, and invoice verification. Rather than an AI agent seeing isolated records, the Knowledge Graph lets it understand the relationships and rules that govern how your business actually operates.

For existing SAP customers, this is a significant advantage. Years of business logic already embedded in your SAP systems — processes, hierarchies, policies, and relationships — can be surfaced through the Knowledge Graph and made available to AI agents. This means your AI does not start from scratch. It starts with a deep, structured understanding of your business built on the data and processes you already run.

The practical outcome: AI agents powered by BDC and the Knowledge Graph can answer questions, orchestrate workflows, and make recommendations that are grounded in your real business context — reducing hallucination, improving reliability, and delivering decisions that actually make sense for your organisation.

entry.title: Building Your First Data Product in SAP Datasphere: Step-by-Step Practical Guide
entry.content:
SAP Datasphere - End-to-End Data Product Creation Guide for Beginners

Beginner Implementation Guide

This article provides a complete step-by-step implementation guide to create a Data Product in SAP Datasphere, starting from the initial Space creation until publishing and consuming the final Data Product.

Target Audience: SAP Consultants, Data Engineers, Analytics Consultants, and beginners who want to understand SAP Datasphere Data Products.

Introduction

SAP Datasphere is SAP's strategic cloud data management platform that enables organizations to integrate, model, govern, and share trusted business data.

It provides capabilities for data integration, semantic modeling, data governance, and controlled data sharing across enterprise applications.

What is a Data Product?

A Data Product is a governed and reusable data asset that combines technical data objects with business metadata, ownership information, documentation, and controlled access.

Instead of sharing raw technical data, organizations can publish trusted business-ready datasets that can be discovered and consumed by different users and applications.

Why Companies Create Data Products

  • Improve enterprise data governance
  • Create trusted and reusable datasets
  • Enable easier data discovery
  • Support self-service analytics
  • Reduce repeated data preparation activities
  • Create a controlled data-sharing approach

Difference Between Table, View, Analytical Model, and Data Product

Object Description

TableA physical data storage object containing raw or processed business data.
ViewA modeled representation of data created from one or more tables.
Analytical ModelA semantic business model optimized for analytical consumption.
Data ProductA governed and publishable data asset containing metadata, ownership, and technical artifacts.

Data Product Lifecycle

The complete lifecycle implemented in this guide:

Space
↓
Table + Data
↓
Graphical View
↓
Expose for Consumption
↓
Deploy View
↓
Context Management
↓
Data Provider Profile
↓
Data Product Creation
↓
Product Artifact
↓
Publish Data Product
↓
Consumption

Architecture Overview

The following architecture represents the relationship between source data and final consumers:

Source Data
↓
SAP Datasphere Space
↓
Table
↓
View
↓
Data Product
↓
Consumer

Step 1 - Create SAP Datasphere Space

Navigation

SAP Datasphere → Space Management

What is a Space?

A Space is a logical working environment inside SAP Datasphere where data models, tables, views, and other objects are created and managed.

Spaces provide:

  • Data storage allocation
  • User and role management
  • Security control
  • Development environment separation

Implementation Steps

  1. Open Space Management
  2. Select Create Space
  3. Enter Space Name
  4. Add Description
  5. Configure Storage
  6. Assign Users and Roles
  7. Deploy and Activate Space

Example Configuration

Space NameSALES_SPACE
DescriptionSales Analytics Data Space
PurposeCreate and publish sales-related Data Products

Common Mistakes

  • Creating objects in the wrong Space
  • Not assigning required users and roles
  • Incorrect storage configuration
  • Not activating the Space after creation

Step 2 - Create Table and Load Data

Navigation

SAP Datasphere → Data Builder

Create Example Table

Table Name: SALES_DATA

Column Data Type Description

SALES_IDIntegerUnique Sales Transaction ID
CUSTOMERStringCustomer Name
PRODUCTStringProduct Name
AMOUNTDecimal(10,2)Sales Amount
SALES_DATEDateTransaction Date


Important Database Concepts

Primary Key:

A unique identifier that prevents duplicate records and identifies each business transaction.

Precision and Scale:

Precision defines the total number of digits stored, while scale defines the number of digits after the decimal point.

Example:

Decimal(10,2)

Means:

  • Total digits: 10
  • Decimal digits: 2

CSV Import Process

  1. Prepare CSV file with correct column structure
  2. Upload the file into SAP Datasphere
  3. Map CSV columns with table columns
  4. Validate data types
  5. Execute Import

Sample Sales Data

SALES_ID CUSTOMER PRODUCT AMOUNT SALES_DATE

1ABC CompanyLaptop1500.002026-09-01
2XYZ CompanyMonitor500.002026-09-02

Best Practices

  • Always validate source data before loading
  • Define correct data types before import
  • Avoid using insufficient decimal precision
  • Maintain clear naming conventions

Step 3 - Create Graphical View

Navigation

SAP Datasphere → Data Builder → New → Graphical View

What is a Graphical View?

A Graphical View is a data modeling object that allows consultants to transform technical tables into business-oriented datasets.

Views can include:

  • Column selection
  • Filtering
  • Calculated fields
  • Joins between different data sources
  • Business logic transformation

Create Example View

View Name: V_SALES_DATA

Implementation Steps

  1. Open Data Builder
  2. Select New → Graphical View
  3. Add SALES_DATA table as source
  4. Select required columns
  5. Create projection
  6. Save the View

Why is the View Required Before Creating a Data Product?

Data Products are designed to expose business-ready and governed data assets, not raw technical tables.

The View provides a semantic layer where data can be prepared, controlled, and optimized before publishing.

Example View Structure

Source Table View Output

SALES_DATAV_SALES_DATA
Raw Transaction DataBusiness Ready Sales Dataset

Best Practices

  • Use meaningful naming conventions.
  • Avoid exposing unnecessary columns.
  • Apply business rules inside the modeling layer.
  • Document the purpose of every view.

Step 4 - Enable Expose for Consumption

What Does Expose for Consumption Mean?

Expose for Consumption makes the View available for external consumption scenarios and allows it to be used as an artifact inside a Data Product.

Before Enabling Consumption

The View exists only inside the SAP Datasphere modeling environment.

After Enabling Consumption

The View becomes available for governed sharing and Data Product creation.

Steps

  1. Open View Properties
  2. Locate Consumption Settings
  3. Enable:
    Expose for Consumption = ON
  4. Save changes

Important Notes

  • Only approved business-ready Views should be exposed.
  • Exposure does not automatically publish the data.
  • Deployment is still required before consumption.

Step 5 - Deploy View

Why Deployment is Required

SAP Datasphere separates design-time objects from runtime objects.

Deployment activates the View and makes it available for execution and consumption.

Deployment Steps

  1. Save the View
  2. Select Deploy
  3. Wait for deployment completion
  4. Validate deployment status

Expected Result

Status: Deployed

Common Deployment Issues

  • Missing permissions
  • Invalid source objects
  • Incomplete modeling changes
  • Inactive dependencies

Step 6 - Create Context

Navigation

SAP Datasphere → Data Sharing Cockpit → Context Management

What is a Context?

A Context defines the business environment where Data Products are organized, managed, and shared.

Contexts help consumers understand the business area and ownership of published data.

Create Example Context

Context NameAnalytics
TypeInternal Data Marketplace
RoleOwner
StatusActive

Implementation Steps

  1. Open Context Management
  2. Select Create Context
  3. Enter Context Information
  4. Assign Owner
  5. Activate Context

Best Practices

  • Create contexts based on business domains.
  • Define clear ownership.
  • Avoid creating too many unnecessary contexts.

Step 7 - Create Data Provider Profile

Navigation

Data Sharing Cockpit → My Data Provider Profile

What is a Data Provider Profile?

A Data Provider Profile represents the organization or business unit responsible for publishing Data Products.

It provides business identity information for consumers who discover and use Data Products.

Example Provider Profile

Business NameGE371426 Sales Provider
Technical NameSALES_PROVIDER
VisibilityInternal Data Provider
IndustryRetail

Provider Profile Fields

  • Business Name: Display name shown to consumers.
  • Technical Name: System identifier.
  • Description: Explains provider responsibility.
  • Visibility: Defines who can discover the provider.
  • Industry: Business classification.
  • Contact Information: Responsible communication details.

Implementation Steps

  1. Open My Data Provider Profile
  2. Create Provider Profile
  3. Maintain business information
  4. Save and activate profile

Best Practices

  • Keep provider information accurate.
  • Assign clear ownership.
  • Maintain consistent naming standards.

Step 8 - Create Data Product

Navigation

SAP Datasphere → Data Sharing Cockpit → My Data Products → Create

What is a Data Product?

A Data Product is the final governed data asset that combines business metadata, ownership information, documentation, and technical artifacts.

It allows consumers to discover and use trusted business data without directly accessing technical objects.

Create Example Data Product

Product NameSALES_DATA_PRODUCT
Product IDSALES_DATA_PRODUCT
ContextAnalytics
Data CategoryBusiness Data
IndustryRetail

Product Metadata

Product metadata describes the business meaning and purpose of the Data Product.

  • Business description
  • Data ownership
  • Business domain
  • Classification information
  • Usage purpose

Lifecycle Status

Data Products move through different lifecycle stages:

Draft
↓
Listed
↓
Published

Implementation Steps

  1. Open My Data Products
  2. Select Create
  3. Enter Product Information
  4. Assign Context
  5. Maintain Metadata
  6. Save Product

Best Practices

  • Use meaningful business names.
  • Provide clear descriptions.
  • Define ownership before publishing.
  • Avoid exposing technical objects without business context.

Step 9 - Add Product Artifact

What is a Product Artifact?

A Product Artifact is the technical object delivered as part of the Data Product.

In our example, the artifact is the deployed View:

SALES_DATA_PRODUCT
↓
V_SALES_DATA

Relationship Between Product and Artifact

Object Purpose

Data ProductBusiness-facing governed data asset
ArtifactTechnical data object delivered to consumers
ViewActual dataset consumed by applications

Implementation Steps

  1. Open Data Product
  2. Navigate to Product Artifacts
  3. Select Add Artifact
  4. Choose V_SALES_DATA View
  5. Save Changes

Important Checks

  • View must be deployed.
  • Expose for Consumption must be enabled.
  • Artifact assignment must be completed successfully.

Step 10 - Publish / List Data Product

Data Product Lifecycle

Draft
↓
Listed
↓
Published

Publishing Steps

  1. Open Data Product
  2. Validate metadata
  3. Check artifact availability
  4. Change lifecycle status
  5. Publish the Data Product

Expected Result

The Data Product becomes available for consumers according to the configured sharing rules.

Before Publishing Validate:

  • Correct business description
  • Correct ownership
  • Valid artifact assignment
  • Successful deployment

Implementation Experience and Lessons Learned

During this implementation, I learned that creating a Data Product in SAP Datasphere is not only about creating technical objects and publishing them. The most important part is preparing the data asset correctly for business consumption.

One of the key points during the implementation was ensuring that the Graphical View was properly configured before using it as a Data Product artifact. The View needed to be deployed and exposed for consumption before it became available for sharing.

Another important observation was that Data Product creation requires both technical and business information. Technical objects alone are not sufficient; metadata, ownership, context, and description are required to make the Data Product understandable and reusable for consumers.

This implementation helped me understand the complete lifecycle from data modeling to governed data sharing.

Testing and Validation

Before considering the implementation complete, validate every lifecycle component.

Check Status

Space Active☐
Table Created and Loaded☐
View Created☐
Expose for Consumption Enabled☐
View Deployed☐
Context Active☐
Provider Profile Created☐
Artifact Added☐
Data Product Published☐

Consumer Validation

A consumer should be able to:

  • Discover the Data Product
  • Understand the business meaning
  • Access available data according to permissions
  • Use the dataset for analytics scenarios

Troubleshooting

1. Numeric Overflow During CSV Upload

Cause:

The target column precision is smaller than the incoming data values.

Solution:

  • Increase Decimal Precision.
  • Review source data format.
  • Validate large numeric values before import.

2. View Not Appearing in Data Product

Check the following:

  • Expose for Consumption is enabled.
  • View deployment completed successfully.
  • Artifact is assigned to the Data Product.
  • User has required permissions.

3. Views Count Shows Zero

Possible reasons:

  • No View artifact has been assigned.
  • View is not deployed.
  • Object is not released or available for sharing.
  • Tenant capability limitations.

4. Trial Tenant vs Enterprise Tenant

SAP Datasphere Trial environments are designed for learning and testing.

Enterprise tenants usually provide additional capabilities such as:

  • Enterprise security configuration
  • Advanced integration scenarios
  • Production-grade governance
  • Larger storage and user management options

5. Artifact Not Available During Data Product Creation

Issue:

While creating the Data Product, the required View was not available in the artifact selection list.

Root Cause:

The View was created successfully, but it was not ready for consumption.

Resolution:

  • Verified that Expose for Consumption was enabled.
  • Confirmed that the View was deployed successfully.
  • Checked that the required permissions were available.

After completing these steps, the View became available as a Data Product artifact.

Final Summary

The complete SAP Datasphere Data Product implementation flow:

Space
↓
Table
↓
Data
↓
View
↓
Expose for Consumption
↓
Deploy
↓
Context
↓
Data Provider Profile
↓
Data Product
↓
Artifact
↓
Publish
↓
Consumption

Conclusion

Creating Data Products in SAP Datasphere requires combining technical data modeling with business governance, data sharing concepts, and proper lifecycle management.

By following this lifecycle, SAP consultants can build trusted, reusable, and discoverable data assets that support modern analytics and enterprise data strategies.

During this implementation journey, I learned that successful Data Product creation is not only about creating views and publishing data, but also about understanding artifacts, releases, delivery modes, and consumption scenarios.

From this implementation, I realized that the biggest challenge is not creating individual objects, but connecting all lifecycle steps together. A successful Data Product requires alignment between data modeling, governance, metadata management, and consumer requirements.

Hands-on experience is essential to understand how SAP Datasphere Data Products work in real-world scenarios. I hope this guide helps beginners build a stronger foundation and avoid common challenges when starting their Data Product journey.

entry.title: Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent?
entry.content:
Agent Ready Data Series

01  From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data

02  Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent

03  Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas

A customer may have a governed purchase order data product and ask whether it can be used to build an agent. My answer would be to look first at what the agent is expected to do. Imagine an agent helping a procurement team with delayed orders. A user asks why an order is late and what should happen next.

 

Figure: The five readiness checks for a purchase order data product.

Five checks before the agent uses it

First, define the business meaning. Does late refer to the original delivery date or the latest confirmed date? Is a partially delivered item late? Which status is authoritative? These questions sound basic until an agent has to explain an exception without a buyer beside it.

Second, map the context. The answer may depend on the supplier, contract, goods receipt and current delivery commitment. If that commitment is in an inaccessible email, the agent should say its information is incomplete.

Third, check trust. When were the records updated? Are the fields complete? Can we trace the figures to their source? An unposted goods receipt can make the order look late even when the goods have arrived.

Fourth, test access end to end. A buyer may see only orders within a purchasing organization. The agent’s data access and every tool call must respect the relevant scope. SAP Datasphere data access controls can help restrict rows in protected objects, but the complete path still needs to be tested.

Fifth, define the action. Explaining a delay, recommending a supplier call, creating a task and changing a purchase order have different consequences. The right to read an order is not the right to change it.

A useful starting outcome

I would start with an agent that explains the exception, shows its evidence and points out missing information. Procurement users can then assess whether the result is dependable. Once that works, the business can define which follow-up actions are appropriate and where approval belongs.

The architecture question is not simply whether a data product exists. It is whether the data product and its surrounding context are fit for the exact decision and level of autonomy we expect.

For the purchase order pilot, I would ask the buyer to walk through two real exceptions. One should have complete records; the other should include a missing or conflicting commitment. Those cases show whether the agent can explain uncertainty rather than turn an incomplete picture into a confident instruction.

The same review should include the user experience. If an agent lacks the contract, it should tell the buyer what it checked and suggest who can confirm the commitment. That response is still useful. It respects the limit of the available information and helps the person complete the work.

entry.title: Migrating Existing SQL Queries to SQL View Gateway: A Practical Guide
entry.content:
The first post in this series introduced SQL View Gateway and why it exists. The second post covered how to set it up end to end. The third post walked through connecting to SAP Datasphere and SAP Analytics Cloud.

When I wrote that this series would cover three posts, I did not anticipate the question that keeps coming up from teams moving from on-premise SAP Commerce to SAP Commerce Cloud: I already have SQL queries. How much do I need to rewrite? It deserves its own post.

The short answer is: less than you might expect. This post walks through the six areas where on-premise queries typically need to change, explains what each change looks like in practice, and shows patterns that can reduce the amount of query logic you need to touch.

The context: direct database access on on-premise

On-premise SAP Commerce installations gave teams direct read access to the underlying database. Over time, many teams built integrations — in various services, ETL pipelines, reporting tools — that query this database directly. These queries know the raw table names, column names, join patterns, and internal structures of the SAP Commerce database.

Moving to SAP Commerce Cloud removes direct database access. SQL View Gateway is the supported, governed equivalent — it provides read-only SQL access to SAP Commerce Cloud data, with role-based access control, TLS encryption, and a full audit trail. But it exposes data through the SAP Commerce type system, not as raw database tables.

That difference is real, but for most queries the practical impact is smaller than it first appears.

Area 1: Table and column names

Raw table names in the on-premise SAP Commerce database (orders, products) become view names derived from the SAP Commerce Cloud type system, combining the role name and the type name: salesreporting_order, salesreporting_product.

Column names within view follow the SAP Commerce Cloud attribute name rather than the raw database column name (which is typically prefixed with p_). So p_code becomes code, p_deliverycost becomes deliveryCost, createdTS becomes creationtime.

The mapping is deterministic. You can extract it for any set of types directly from your SAP Commerce Cloud system using the following FlexibleSearch query, run in HAC (Console → FlexibleSearch):

SELECT {tc.code}, {ad.qualifier}, {ad.databaseColumn}
FROM {AttributeDescriptor AS ad
  JOIN ComposedType AS tc ON {ad.enclosingType} = {tc.pk}}
WHERE {tc.code} IN ('Order', 'OrderEntry', 'Product', 'Category')
ORDER BY {tc.code}, {ad.qualifier}

Replace the type list with the types relevant to your migration. The result gives you the complete mapping from SAP Commerce Cloud attribute name (the SQL View Gateway view column name) to the underlying database column name (what your current queries reference). With that mapping in hand, adapting your queries is a find-and-replace operation — systematic, not a rewrite.

Area 2: Relations

For 1:1 and 1:N relations, SAP Commerce Cloud stores a foreign key attribute directly on the item — a column holding the PK of the referenced item. SQL View Gateway exposes that column directly. If your current query does:

SELECT e.*, o.p_status
FROM orderentries e
JOIN orders o ON o.PK = e.p_order

The SQL View Gateway equivalent is structurally identical:

SELECT e.*, o.status
FROM salesreporting_orderentry e
JOIN salesreporting_order o ON o.pk = e.order

The join logic and PK-based navigation carry over unchanged. Only the names differ.

For N:N relations, SAP Commerce Cloud creates a dedicated relation type — for example, CategoryProductRelation — which on-premise SAP Commerce backed with a table (e.g. cat2prodrel) containing p_source and p_target columns. This relation type can be exposed through SQL View Gateway like any other type, producing a view with source and target columns containing PKs:

data-extraction.role-based-config.salesreporting.types=Product,Category,CategoryProductRelation
data-extraction.role-based-config.salesreporting.CategoryProductRelation.attributes=source,target

To find the exact name of the relation type between any two types, and confirm which side is source and which is target, run the following FlexibleSearch query in HAC (Console → FlexibleSearch):

SELECT {relType.code} AS 'relation.typeCode', {srcType.code} AS 'source.typeCode', {tgtType.code} AS 'target.typeCode'
FROM {AttributeDescriptor AS src
  JOIN AttributeDescriptor AS tgt ON {src.enclosingType} = {tgt.enclosingType}
  JOIN ComposedType AS relType ON {src.enclosingType} = {relType.pk}
  JOIN ComposedType AS srcType ON {src.attributeType} = {srcType.pk}
  JOIN ComposedType AS tgtType ON {tgt.attributeType} = {tgtType.pk}}
WHERE {src.qualifier} = 'source'
  AND {tgt.qualifier} = 'target'
  AND 'Product' IN ({srcType.code}, {tgtType.code})
  AND 'Category' IN ({srcType.code}, {tgtType.code})

Replace 'Product' and 'Category' with the two types you are interested in. For example, the relation between Product and Category resolves to CategoryProductRelation, with Category as the source and Product as the target.

Ordered relations

If a relation is ordered, SAP Commerce Cloud stores the position as a sequenceNumber attribute on the relation type. This is a regular attribute — expose it in your role configuration like any other:

data-extraction.role-based-config.salesreporting.CategoryProductRelation.attributes=source,target,sequenceNumber

Your existing ORDER BY logic based on sequence can then reference the sequenceNumber column directly from the view.

Legacy and custom-persistence relation types

Some older or custom relation types use a persistence mechanism that does not produce a standard item deployment — for example, types that use Link as their persistence class or that declare no <deployment> in items.xml. SQL View Gateway validates every type against its deployment before creating a view. A type with no deployment is silently skipped, with a warning in the deployment log.

If a relation type you expect to see is missing from the gateway, the deployment log is the first place to check. These types cannot be exposed through SQL View Gateway in their current form.

Area 3: Multiple subtypes in one table

In on-premise SAP Commerce, types that extend a common base type often share a single database table, distinguished by a TypePkString discriminator column. SQL View Gateway creates a separate view per type in SAP Commerce Cloud. If your queries need to identify the subtype of each row, the discriminator is available as the itemtype attribute — expose it in your role configuration like any other attribute.

If your queries operate across the full type hierarchy, the simplest path is to expose the common supertype through SQL View Gateway — the parent type's view includes rows of all its subtypes, so the query structure is unchanged.

If you need to combine specific subtypes that do not share a useful supertype, a Common Table Expression (CTE) reconstructs the equivalent of the shared table as a one-time wrapper at the top of the query:

WITH combined_type AS (
  SELECT pk, code, name, creationtime, modifiedtime FROM salesreporting_subtype1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT pk, code, name, creationtime, modifiedtime FROM salesreporting_subtype2
)
-- your existing query continues unchanged below this line:
SELECT * FROM combined_type WHERE ...

Area 4: Enumeration values

If your queries join to enumeration tables to resolve enum codes or display labels, EnumerationValue is a standard SAP Commerce Cloud type and can be exposed through SQL View Gateway like any other. A view on EnumerationValue with attributes code and name gives you a lookup table that your existing joins can reference — both by PK (for foreign key references stored on items) and by code.

Area 5: Localized attributes

This is the one area where there is a genuine structural difference, and it is worth understanding clearly.

On-premise, localized attributes are stored in separate LP tables (for example, productslp). Each row in an LP table holds the values of all localized attributes of a given item in a given language — one row per item per language. Queries that need localized values join to the LP table and filter by language PK.

SQL View Gateway flattens this structure: localized attributes become columns on the view row, one column per attribute per configured language. This gives you two migration paths.

Option A — implicit locale column

If your queries work with a single language, you can configure SQL View Gateway to expose localized attributes without a language qualifier:

data-extraction.role-based-config.salesreporting.Product.attributes=PK,code,name,description

The system detects that name and description are localized for Product and automatically fetches them in the default language (English by default, configurable via data-extraction.view.localized.default-language in local.properties). The view column is named name — no language suffix.

Your query goes from:

SELECT p.p_code, lp.p_name
FROM products p
JOIN productslp lp ON lp.ITEMPK = p.PK AND lp.LANGPK = 8796093055008

to:

SELECT code, name
FROM salesreporting_product

The join to the LP table disappears entirely. This path simplifies the query significantly, but requires reviewing and restructuring each affected query individually — which carries effort and a risk of introducing errors.

Option B — CTE wrapper preserving LP table structure

If you want to avoid restructuring individual queries, you can add a CTE at the top that reconstructs the (ITEMPK, value, LANGPK) structure your existing queries already know how to work with. This requires configuring SQL View Gateway to expose multiple language variants explicitly:

data-extraction.role-based-config.salesreporting.Product.attributes=PK,code,name[en],name[pl]

The CTE then reconstructs the LP table structure:

WITH productslp AS (
  SELECT pk AS ITEMPK, name_en AS p_name, 8796093055008 AS LANGPK
  FROM salesreporting_product WHERE name_en IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT pk AS ITEMPK, name_pl AS p_name, 8796093546528 AS LANGPK
  FROM salesreporting_product WHERE name_pl IS NOT NULL
)
-- your existing query continues unchanged below this line:
SELECT p.pk, lp.p_name
FROM salesreporting_product p
JOIN productslp lp ON lp.ITEMPK = p.pk AND lp.LANGPK = 8796093055008

Note that LANGPK in SAP Commerce Cloud is a numeric PK of the Language record — not a language code string. The values above are examples; the actual PKs in your system can be found by querying the Language type in HAC.

Option B lets you migrate queries mechanically rather than analytically. The trade-off is performance: a CTE adds overhead compared to a direct column read. The recommended approach is to treat it as a stepping stone — use CTEs to unblock the initial migration, then replace them with Option A as time allows, query by query.

The two options can be applied selectively: straightforward queries converted to Option A immediately, complex queries wrapped with Option B and optimised later.

Area 6: Unoptimized attributes

In SAP Commerce Cloud, most attributes are optimized — they have a dedicated column in the SAP Commerce Cloud database structures. Some attributes are unoptimized: they have no dedicated column and are stored separately - you may know them from *props tables (for example, productprops) in the on-premise SAP Commerce database, keyed by item PK and attribute name.

On-premise queries that read unoptimized attributes typically join directly to the *props table:

SELECT p.p_code, pr.VALUESTRING1 AS remarks
FROM products p
JOIN productprops pr ON pr.ITEMPK = p.PK AND pr.NAME = 'remarks'

SQL View Gateway handles unoptimized attributes transparently — they appear in the view as regular columns, with no extra configuration required.. From the outside, remarks appears as a regular column:

SELECT code, remarks
FROM salesreporting_product

This is a simplification — but like localized attributes, it requires analysis and restructuring of each affected query. The *props table join disappears, and the column is read directly from the view. Where restructuring the query is not immediately practical, a CTE can bridge the gap by reconstructing the (ITEMPK, NAME, VALUE) structure:

WITH productprops AS (
  SELECT pk AS ITEMPK, 'remarks' AS NAME, remarks AS VALUESTRING1
  FROM salesreporting_product WHERE remarks IS NOT NULL
)
-- your existing query continues unchanged below this line:
SELECT p.p_code, pr.VALUESTRING1 AS remarks
FROM salesreporting_product p
JOIN productprops pr ON pr.ITEMPK = p.pk AND pr.NAME = 'remarks'

As with localized attributes, treat the CTE approach as a stepping stone — it unblocks migration without requiring immediate query restructuring, but carries a performance cost and should be replaced with direct column reads over time.

What SQL View Gateway does not expose

Not every attribute in the SAP Commerce Cloud type system is available through SQL View Gateway. Beyond the security-related block list described in the second post in this series, the system automatically skips attributes that cannot be meaningfully represented as SQL columns:

  • Attributes with no database column — computed or virtual attributes that exist only in the service layer, with no backing column in the database
  • Encrypted attributes — values encrypted at the persistence layer are not exposed
  • Attributes typed as java.lang.Object — serialized Java objects stored as binary blobs have no SQL-readable representation
  • Collections with non-exportable element types — collections whose elements are complex Java objects rather than primitive or standard types

All of these are silently skipped during view generation, with a warning written to the deployment log. If an attribute you expect to see is missing from a view, reviewing the deployment log is the first step.

The bigger picture

Each of the five areas above has a mechanical migration path. Table and column renaming is a find-and-replace exercise, aided by the FlexibleSearch mapping query. Relations are structurally equivalent — the join logic does not change. Subtypes and enumerations are covered by either exposing the supertype or using a CTE wrapper. Localized attributes have two practical options depending on how much query restructuring you want to take on upfront.

Moving from on-premise SAP Commerce to SAP Commerce Cloud removes direct database access — and with it, the foundation that existing SQL-based integrations rely on. Without SQL View Gateway, the options may not be attractive: rewrite existing integrations to use OData or another API-based approach, build and maintain a custom data replication layer, or synchronize data to a separate database that your team operates. SQL View Gateway is a different answer: keep your SQL-based integration approach, adapt the queries to the view model, and get role-based access control, TLS, and a full audit trail as part of the deal — maintained by SAP, not by your team.

What's next

If you are planning a migration and have queries that do not obviously fit one of the patterns above, drop a comment below — concrete cases are the most useful input for making this guide better.

entry.title: Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas
entry.content:
Agent Ready Data Series :

01  From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data

02  Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent

03  Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas

 

When a customer says a data product is ready, I like to ask who will answer when an agent gives the wrong answer. The schema may be clear and the pipeline may run every day. But if a business definition changes or a source starts arriving late, somebody must own that change.

 

Figure: The owner remains accountable for changes and exceptions after a data product is published.

Treat the interface as a product

Take a supplier performance data product. Its consumers may include a dashboard, a sourcing analyst and an agent that recommends which supplier needs attention. Each consumer needs to know the unit of analysis, refresh schedule, permitted use, expected quality and contact for an issue. A table name and column list tell only part of that story.

I would define a small product agreement: business purpose, owner, source systems, grain, measure definitions, freshness target, quality rules, sensitivity and access method. I would also describe what happens when the schema or a business rule changes. These are design choices for the team that publishes and consumes the data, not properties I would assume exist automatically.

The agent changes the support model

A human analyst may notice a missing country or an unusual supplier name and investigate. An agent might continue to the next step before anyone notices. That makes ownership and change communication more urgent. If a quality rule fails, should the agent stop, answer with a warning or route the case to a person? The data product owner and process owner should decide together.

SAP Business Data Cloud provides a data product approach, and the catalog helps users find and inspect the assets available to them. My recommendation is to add a clear operating agreement around each high-value product used by agents. Start with one use case, test the agreement with its consumers, then reuse what works in the next domain.

The strongest sign of a mature data product is not that it has been published. It is that a consumer knows what it means, whether it can be trusted today and who will resolve an issue tomorrow.

This also changes how I measure success. I would track whether consumers can find the product, understand its scope and resolve an issue without a long chain of emails. An agent pilot is a good stress test because it exposes unclear ownership quickly.

The product owner should also hear how the agent is being used. If users repeatedly ask questions the product cannot answer, that is input for the product roadmap. If an agent frequently stops because a field arrives late, the owner can prioritize that issue with the source team. Consumption feedback should improve the product.
